svg.title: The three OSPF PE-CE mechanisms: the DN bit, the domain ID and the sham link
svg.desc: Topology of CE1, PE1, the MPLS core, PE2 and CE2 with a backdoor link between the two CEs. Three numbered problems are marked along the path. Problem one, a type-3 summary originating in the core is re-injected into OSPF at the other side and can loop, solved by the DN bit which marks routes that already came from a PE. Problem two, when two PEs use different domain IDs the DN bit is honoured inconsistently and routes oscillate, so the domain ID must match across the whole VPN. Problem three, the backdoor link is preferred only in the wrong direction: OSPF prefers intra-area over inter-area, so the backdoor route to a remote site can beat the VPN path, and the sham link advertises the remote prefix as intra-area to make the comparison fair. A right panel gives the three prerequisites for a sham link: matching area, matching authentication and a loopback to loopback tunnel.
svg.text: OSPF across an L3VPN needs three mechanisms because OSPF trusts topology it cannot see
DN bit stops loops, domain ID keeps that decision consistent, sham link fixes the priority inversion
CE1
PE1
MPLS core
PE2
CE2
backdoor link between the two CEs
THE THREE PROBLEMS, IN THE ORDER THEY BITE
1. Re-injection loop
A summary learned from the core comes back
into OSPF at the far PE and can circle.
Fix: DN bit marks routes already carried
by a PE, and those are never re-advertised.
2. Domain ID mismatch
Each PE sets a domain ID; the DN bit is only
honoured for its own domain. If two PEs in
one VPN disagree, routes oscillate.
Fix: one domain ID per VPN, no exceptions.
3. Priority inversion
OSPF prefers intra-area > inter-area > external,
so the backdoor intra-area path can beat the
VPN path regardless of cost.
Fix: sham link makes the VPN path look intra-area.
A sham link needs three things to come up
1. Both endpoints in the same OSPF area.
2. Matching authentication, or it stays down.
3. A loopback-to-loopback path through the MPLS VPN, not through the core IGP.
The honest alternative
If the backdoor exists for resilience, an eBGP PE-CE design removes all three problems at
once, because BGP compares equal metrics across domains by design. Use OSPF at the
PE-CE only when the customer's operations require it.
Verification: read the OSPF database on both PEs, confirm the remote prefix carries the DN bit and the same domain ID, then check which path the SPF actually installed.
